# OPERATIONS IMPROVEMENT PLAN: LEAD TIME REDUCTION WITHOUT QUALITY COMPROMISE

## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

**Strategic Challenge:** 14-week quoted lead time vs. competitor's 6 weeks is losing 33% of deals. Prior compression attempt failed (warranty spike), eroding trust in lead-time reduction. Three functions (Production, Quality, Sales) lack alignment on root causes and solutions.

**Diagnostic Finding:** Lead time loss is concentrated in five areas: (1) **Quality gate wait times** (inspections sequenced after production, not concurrent); (2) **Supplier coordination delays** (components arrive out-of-sync; production idle); (3) **Schedule batching** (small orders queued; setup time amortized inefficiently); (4) **Rework loops** (quality failures cause 3-5 day delays; root causes not fixed upstream); (5) **Cross-functional handoff friction** (no shared lead-time accountability; blame cycling).

**Proposed Approach:** Compress lead time to **9-10 weeks** (vs. current 14 weeks) through:
- **Concurrent quality inspections** (quality gates embedded in production line, not downstream verification)
- **Supplier synchronization** (demand planning 12-week rolling window; supplier line-item confirmation 8 weeks out)
- **Batch-size optimization** (reduce lot size; increase scheduling frequency; absorb setup cost in overhead)
- **Root-cause rework prevention** (SPC/process capability tracking; first-pass yield target 98%+)
- **Shared metrics & governance** (single "lead time" KPI; weekly cross-functional ops council; incentives aligned to lead time + quality)

**Quality Protection:** Embed inspections *into* production workflow (in-process control) rather than *after* production (downstream verification). Certified quality maintained or improved because: (1) defects caught immediately (no rework delay); (2) root causes visible to production (process adjustment immediate); (3) SPC data predicts failures before they occur. **Warranty claims expected to *decrease* vs. current baseline.**

**Business Impact:**
- **Lead time:** 14 weeks → 9-10 weeks (36-43% reduction) → win back 1 of 3 lost deals (~$8-12M incremental annual revenue at typical ASP)
- **Quality:** Current certification maintained; warranty claims decrease 15-20% (from faster detection + root-cause fix)
- **Profitability:** Lead-time compression + warranty reduction + capacity unlock (same plant ships 20% more) → incremental $2-4M EBITDA annually

---

## PART 1: ROOT CAUSE DIAGNOSIS – WHERE TIME IS ACTUALLY LOST

### 1.1 CURRENT STATE PROCESS MAP & TIME ANALYSIS

**Objective:** Map full production + quality + logistics cycle; quantify time at each stage; identify waste.

---

#### 1.1.1 Current Process Map with Time Breakdown (14-Week Baseline)

**Assumption:** Industrial equipment manufacturer; products are mid-complexity (e.g., pumps, compressors, control systems); ~8-12 week production + 2-3 week logistics/buffer typical in industry.

| Process Stage | Current Duration | % of Total Lead Time | Activity Description | Constraint / Bottleneck |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SALES & CONFIGURATION (Week 0)** | 2-3 days | 1-2% | Customer specifies requirements; sales engineer configures BOM; customer approves; order entered into MRP | Sales → Eng handoff delays; BOM changes after entry (1 in 3 orders modified post-entry) |
| **SUPPLIER PROCUREMENT (Week 0-3)** | 2-3 weeks | 14-21% | PO issued to suppliers; long-lead items (motors, specialty materials) ordered; delivery tracked | **Major bottleneck:** Suppliers quote 8-10 week lead times; components arrive out-of-sync (some early, some late); production waits for critical path item |
| **PRODUCTION QUEUE & SETUP (Week 3-4)** | 1-2 weeks | 7-14% | Batch of orders accumulated in queue; setup for first job (tooling, fixtures, operator training); first unit produced | Schedule driven by order size + date; small orders queued behind large ones; setup amortized over batch |
| **MACHINING / FABRICATION (Week 4-8)** | 3-4 weeks | 21-29% | Primary production (cutting, forming, assembly subcomponents); materials processed in sequence | Process times standardized; little waste; **constraint is batching logic (setup amortization over batch size)** |
| **ASSEMBLY (Week 8-10)** | 2 weeks | 14% | Subcomponents assembled into final product; partial testing (electrical continuity, mechanical fit) | Dependent on **all supplier components arriving**; if one component late, assembly queued; no early-completion incentive |
| **QUALITY INSPECTION & CERTIFICATION (Week 10-12)** | 1.5-2 weeks | 11-14% | **Post-production quality gates:** Full inspection, calibration, certified testing (pressure, performance); documentation for compliance | **CRITICAL BOTTLENECK:** Inspections begin only after assembly complete; defects discovered late; rework requires 3-5 days (re-machine, re-assemble, re-test); delays shipment of that unit + downstream orders |
| **REWORK (if needed) (Week 10-13)** | 3-5 days (variable) | 2-4% (but high variance) | If inspection fails, unit returned to production for correction; re-inspection; ~20% of units require minor rework; ~5% require major rework | **Root-cause not systematically addressed:** Same defect types repeat; process capability not tracked upstream |
| **PACKAGING & LOGISTICS (Week 12-14)** | 1-2 weeks | 7-14% | Final packaging, documentation, shipping logistics coordination, delivery scheduling | No compression opportunity here without sacrificing logistics efficiency |
| **TOTAL LEAD TIME** | **14 weeks (98 days)** | **100%** | — | — |

**Key Insight:** Sequential (waterfall) process = ~5 weeks of potential parallelization loss. Quality bottleneck (1.5-2 weeks) occurs *after* all production complete, meaning defects discovered too late.

---

#### 1.1.2 Competitor Benchmarking (6-Week Lead Time)

**Question:** How does competitor achieve 6-week lead time on same product complexity?

**Research Approach:**
- [ ] **Customer interviews (Month 1):** Identify 2-3 customers who buy from both your company and competitor; ask what competitor offers / how they achieve speed
- [ ] **Industry benchmarking (Month 1):** Contact industry associations (ASME, OEM groups); review published lead-time benchmarks for similar products
- [ ] **Reverse-engineering competitor's process (Months 1-2):**
  - Request quote for same product from competitor; document timeline offered
  - If possible, visit competitor facility (industry tour, trade show) or speak with ex-employees; understand their production model
  - Document: Do they pre-stock components? Use modular designs? Outsource assembly? Use concurrent quality?

**Preliminary Hypothesis (based on typical best-in-class practices):**

| Factor | Your Company (14 weeks) | Competitor (6 weeks) | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Supplier coordination** | 8-10 week supplier lead times; order-by-order procurement | 12-week rolling demand forecast; supplier line-item confirmed 8 weeks prior; safety stock of long-lead items | 2-3 weeks |
| **Quality gates** | Sequential (post-production, 1.5-2 weeks) | Concurrent (in-process, inspections embedded; <1 week total) | 1-1.5 weeks |
| **Batch size / scheduling** | Order batches; setup amortized over 10-15 unit batches | Smaller batches (5-8 units); increased setup frequency; setup cost absorbed in standard overhead | 0.5-1 week |
| **Rework delay** | Defects cause 3-5 day rework loops; root causes not fixed | SPC-driven process control; defects prevented upstream; rework rare (<2% of units) | 0.5-1 week |
| **Production queue** | 1-2 week queue from schedule batching | Express queue option for expedited orders (priority fee); standard queue for routine orders | 0.5 week |
| **Supply logistics** | Standard shipping (7-10 days); 1-2 week buffer for delays | Just-in-time inbound; milk-run consolidation; 3-5 day logistics | 0.5-1 week |
| **TOTAL REDUCTION** | — | — | **5-8 weeks** |

**Implication:** Competitor likely uses 3-4 of these tactics (not all 6). Your quickest wins are: (1) Concurrent quality; (2) Supplier synchronization; (3) Batch-size reduction.

---

#### 1.1.3 Last Failed Compression Attempt – Lessons Learned

**What Happened (2-3 years ago):**
- **Initiative:** "Fast Track" program; goal: reduce lead time to 10 weeks
- **Method:** Production pushed to compress schedule; reduce batch sizes; cut quality inspection time
- **Result:** Lead time achieved 10-11 weeks; *but* warranty claims spiked 35-40% in months 4-6; caused customer returns, recalls, brand damage
- **Outcome:** Program abandoned; perception damage lasted 18+ months

**Root Causes of Failure (reconstruct from records/interviews, Month 1):**

1. **Quality gates were compressed (skipped), not embedded:**
   - Intention: "Reduce post-production inspection time by 50%"
   - Implementation: Inspectors told to work faster / reduce sample size
   - Actual result: Defects not caught; reached customer with failures
   - **Why it failed:** You can't inspect quality *into* a product; you have to build it in upstream

2. **Production pushed without process capability data:**
   - Schedule pressure overrode process logic
   - Operators instructed to "maintain quality while going faster" (impossible without process change)
   - Setup times not reduced; batches just small enough to disable amortization
   - **Why it failed:** You can't compress activity without changing the process; faster ≠ same quality if process unchanged

3. **No root-cause prevention system:**
   - Defects identified late (in customer returns, not in production)
   - Quality team blamed production ("they shipped defective units"); Production blamed quality ("they approved bad design")
   - Root causes (material issue, tooling wear, operator training gap) never systematically addressed
   - **Why it failed:** Rework cycle got worse, not better; same defects repeated because fixes were band-aids, not root causes

4. **Sales over-promised; operations under-delivered:**
   - Sales communicated 10-week lead time to customers before feasibility confirmed
   - Operations forced to compress; quality sacrificed to meet sales promise
   - **Why it failed:** No shared accountability; Sales and Operations not aligned on feasibility

**Key Lesson for New Initiative:**
- **DO NOT compress quality gates; instead, embed quality into production (concurrent inspection, SPC)**
- **DO NOT push without process capability data (measure baseline; confirm new process is capable before scaling)**
- **DO NOT promise lead time without ops sign-off (shared Sales-Ops-Quality governance)**

---

### 1.2 CROSS-FUNCTIONAL ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS: WHY SALES, PRODUCTION, QUALITY DON'T ALIGN

#### 1.2.1 Current Organizational Accountability & Incentives

**Problem:** Three functions blame each other for lead-time delays; no single owner; no aligned incentive.

| Function | KPI / Accountability | Incentive Misalignment | Behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SALES** | Revenue; Deal closure rate; Customer satisfaction (CSAT) | Compensated on deals closed, not lead time. Selling speed: "I need 10-week lead time to win deals." | Over-commits on lead time (promises 10 weeks when feasible lead time is 12-13); then blames Operations for delay. Pushes Operations to compress every order individually (vs. systematic improvement). |
| **PRODUCTION** | Cost per unit; throughput; On-time delivery (%) | Incentivized on unit cost, not lead time. Batch size optimization: "Larger batches = lower unit cost." | Defaults to large batches (amortize setup); pushes back on sales expedite requests ("You'll disrupt our schedule"). When lead-time pressure hits, ignores quality protocol to maintain schedule. Blames Quality for "approval delays." |
| **QUALITY** | Defect rate; Audit compliance; Customer returns | Incentivized on defect rate, not lead time. Inspection protocol: "Every unit must pass full certified inspection." | Views expedited orders as risk ("We don't have time for full inspection"). Slow to approve when pressure is on (defensive position). Blames Production for not building to spec; blames Sales for unrealistic expectations. |

**Outcome:** Lead-time improvement blocked by finger-pointing. No shared KPI; no incentive to collaborate.

---

#### 1.2.2 Root Causes of Cross-Functional Friction

**Diagnosis (Months 1-2: Structured interviews with each function)**

**SALES PERSPECTIVE (Interview sample: 3-4 sales engineers + sales manager)**

*"Why can't we offer 9-week lead time like the competitor?"*
- "Production says batching and supplier lead times are constraints."
- "Quality says they need 2 weeks for inspection; if we try to go faster, they say we're compromising safety."
- "We lose deals every month because of lead time. Competitor quotes 6 weeks; we quote 14. Customer picks them 80% of the time on speed alone."
- "When we do push for expedited delivery, production schedules us behind big orders; we slip anyway. And if we slip, it's our fault for over-committing?"

*Underlying assumption:* "Ops is not incentivized to improve lead time. Our KPI is revenue; theirs is cost per unit. They optimize for batch size, not speed."

**PRODUCTION PERSPECTIVE (Interview sample: Plant Manager, Production Engineer, Scheduling)**

*"Why can't we go faster without hurting cost or quality?"*
- "Supplier lead times are 8-10 weeks. We're ordering 12 weeks out, and components still arrive late or out-of-sync. We can't start assembly until critical-path supplier ships."
- "Sales sends us expedited orders with 1-week notice. We're not set up for that volume of setup. Every expedite order disrupts the batch schedule and raises our unit costs."
- "Quality gate at end of line is a bottleneck. 20% of units need rework because of design issues or material problems caught too late. But we can't build faster than Quality can inspect."
- "We batch orders to amortize setup (tooling, jig changeover = 4-6 hours). Smaller batches = more setups = higher unit cost. Finance holds us to cost targets; can't absorb higher setup overhead."

*Underlying assumption:* "Lead time is driven by supplier delays and setup time, not by our process. Sales overpromises. Quality is the bottleneck. We're doing the best we can given the constraints."

**QUALITY PERSPECTIVE (Interview sample: Quality Manager, Inspectors, Test Engineer)**

*"Why is inspection a 2-week bottleneck? Why can't we go faster?"*
- "Certified inspection protocol requires 100% inspection of critical dimensions, pressure/performance testing, and documentation for compliance. We can't skip steps without losing certification."
- "We inherit design flaws from Production (manufacturing capability not verified upstream; operators not trained on new designs). We find defects late (post-assembly), and then Production has to rework."
- "Production ships us units with burrs, material defects, assembly gaps. We spend time troubleshooting root causes instead of just inspecting. If Production built to spec, we could go faster."
- "When Sales pushes for expedited delivery, Production tries to skip quality checks. We refuse; then we're blamed for 'holding up' the order. But we're not going to compromise certification."

*Underlying assumption:* "We're the safeguard against shipping junk. If we go faster, defects reach customers. We're not the bottleneck; poor upstream processes are the bottleneck."

**Cross-Functional Insight:**
- Sales blames Production (batching, supplier lead time)
- Production blames Quality (bottleneck) + Sales (expedite disruption) + Suppliers
- Quality blames Production (defects inherited from poor build)
- **No one takes ownership of lead time as a system problem**

---

#### 1.2.3 Supplier Coordination Root Causes

**Current Supplier Management (Interview with Procurement, Month 1):**

*"How far in advance do you place orders with suppliers?"*
- "We place POs when customer order is received (Week 0), or if inventory is pre-stocked, we order when we're down to safety stock."
- "Suppliers quote 8-10 week lead times. For long-lead items (motors, specialty materials), we're often told 'stock available in 8 weeks; we can expedite to 6 weeks for +15% cost.'"
- "Components arrive out-of-sync. Motor arrives Week 6, but control board arrives Week 8. We have to stage components and wait for critical path before starting assembly."
- "For expedited orders, suppliers want rush fees. But even with rush, we only get 1-2 week improvement."
- "We don't have visibility into supplier capacity. If multiple customers (us + competitor) order at same time, suppliers allocate based on order date. We don't have preferential allocation."

**Root Causes:**
1. **Reactive procurement (order-by-order):** No demand planning shared with suppliers
2. **Supplier lead times = 8-10 weeks:** Suppliers not optimized for shorter cycles
3. **Out-of-sync component delivery:** No synchronization mechanism
4. **No preferred supplier relationships:** All suppliers treat us as transactional customers
5. **No visibility into supplier roadmap:** Can't negotiate capacity reservations or expedited alloc

**Opportunity:** Move from reactive (order-triggered) to proactive (demand forecasted) procurement.

---

### 1.3 SUMMARY: WHERE THE 5 WEEKS OF DELAY IS HIDDEN

**Lead Time Compression Potential Analysis:**

| Lead Time Component | Current Duration | Opportunity | Potential Savings | Implementation Difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Supplier coordination (order-to-receipt)** | 8-10 weeks | Implement 12-week rolling demand forecast; confirm line items 8 weeks out; reserve capacity + safety stock | 2-3 weeks | Medium (requires supplier collaboration + inventory investment) |
| **Quality gate (sequential post-production inspection)** | 1.5-2 weeks | Embed in-process quality checks into production line; reduce end-of-line batch inspection to 1-2 days | 1-1.5 weeks | Medium (requires SPC setup + process redesign; quality initially improves) |
| **Production queue / batch setup** | 1-2 weeks | Reduce batch size; increase scheduling frequency; absorb setup cost in overhead | 0.5-1 week | Medium (requires process change in scheduling + cost absorption) |
| **Rework loops** | 3-5 days (variable) | Prevent defects upstream through SPC; reduce rework to <2% of units | 0.5-1 week | High (requires root-cause discipline + operator training) |
| **Production queue priority / expedite option** | Embedded in batch queue | Create express queue path for time-sensitive orders; premium for expedite | 0.5 week | Low (process change only; no capital required) |
| **TOTAL POTENTIAL SAVINGS** | — | — | **5-6.5 weeks** | — |

**Target Lead Time:** 14 weeks - 5 weeks = **9 weeks** (aggressive but achievable; aligns with competitor benchmark + company stretch target)

## PART 2: DETAILED IMPROVEMENT ROADMAP – DESIGN & IMPLEMENTATION

### 2.1 CONCURRENT QUALITY FRAMEWORK: EMBED INSPECTIONS INTO PRODUCTION

#### 2.1.1 Current vs. Proposed Quality Process

**Current Model (Sequential):**
```
Production → Assembly → End-of-Line Inspection (1.5-2 weeks) → Defects Found → Rework (3-5 days) → Re-inspect → Ship
```

**Problem:**
- Defects found after all value-added work complete
- Rework delay cascades to downstream orders
- Root causes discovered late; process not adjusted

**Proposed Model (Concurrent):**
```
Design → Process FMEA → Pilot Run → SPC Baseline → Production (with in-process checks) → Final Verification (1-2 days) → Ship
```

**Process Flow:**

| Stage | Activity | Quality Gate | Timing | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PRE-PRODUCTION (Weeks -2 to 0)** | FMEA on new/modified design; process capability study (Cpk); operator training on critical parameters | Design sign-off: Cpk ≥ 1.33 for critical dimensions; documented procedure | 2-4 weeks before production start | Design Eng + Quality |
| **SETUP & PILOT (Week 0-1)** | First-piece inspection (FPI); verify tooling, fixtures, process parameters; produce 5-10 pilot units | All critical dimensions measured; SPC chart initiated; process adjusted if out-of-spec | 3-5 days | Production + Quality Tech |
| **IN-PROCESS QUALITY (Weeks 1-3, ongoing)** | **Operator self-inspection:** Every 10th unit (rotating), operator stops line; measures 3-5 critical dimensions; plots on SPC chart. **If out-of-control:** Line stop; root cause addressed (tooling adjustment, material check, parameter reset); resume. **Automated inspection (optional):** Vision systems on conveyor; check for burrs, dimensional variation, missing components | Operator trained on SPC interpretation; SPC limits set (±1σ, ±2σ, ±3σ); out-of-control trigger defined | Continuous during shift | Production Operators + SPC Tech |
| **ASSEMBLY VERIFICATION (Week 2-3)** | Pressure/performance test on sample (every 20th unit); electrical continuity check (all units); fit verification (assembly jigs confirm alignment) | Test results logged; trending on control chart; failures trigger root cause (assembly procedure review, component issue, design gap) | Integrated into assembly line; no queue | Assembly Tech + QA |
| **FINAL CERTIFICATION (Week 3+)** | End-of-line verification (10-20% sample vs. 100% previous); focus on high-risk dimensions/functions; documentation for compliance | Certified test certificate issued; traceability to lot; any failures trigger 100% re-inspection of that lot | 1-2 days (batch of 10-20 units) | Quality Inspector |
| **REWORK (if needed, rare)** | Root cause identified in-process; rework done immediately on production line; no delay to shipment | Next unit + next run; process adjusted to prevent recurrence; Cpk recalculated monthly | Integrated into production cycle | Production + Quality |

**Quality Assurance Maintained:**
- **Certified testing:** Still performed; sample-based (not 100% for routine products) with SPC trending replacing 100% inspection
- **Traceability:** Serial number / lot number tied to each unit; SPC data retained for 5+ years (regulatory requirement)
- **Capability focus:** FMEA + Cpk study upstream ensures process is *capable* of meeting spec before production starts
- **First-pass yield:** Target 98%+ (vs. current ~80%); reduces rework time; faster throughput

**Time Savings:** 1.5-2 weeks (end-of-line inspection batch) → 1-2 days (final certification) = **~10 days saved = 1.4 weeks**

---

#### 2.1.2 SPC (Statistical Process Control) Implementation Plan

**Objective:** Prevent defects upstream (in-process) rather than discover them downstream (post-production).

**Timeline:** Months 1-3 (setup & training); Months 4-12 (pilot on 2-3 product lines); Months 13-24 (scale to all product lines)

**Step 1: Identify Critical-to-Quality (CTQ) Parameters (Month 1)**

| Product Line | Critical Dimension / Function | Spec Range | Current Cpk | Target Cpk | Control Limit (±2σ from mean) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[Product A]** | Bore diameter | 50.00 ± 0.05 mm | ~1.0 (marginal) | 1.5 (strong) | 50.00 ± 0.033 mm |
| **[Product A]** | Pressure rating | 100-120 psi | ~0.9 (weak) | 1.33 (capable) | 100-120 psi range tightened to 105-115 psi |
| **[Product B]** | Runout (concentricity) | <0.03 mm | ~1.1 (marginal) | 1.5 | <0.02 mm |
| **[Product C]** | Electrical resistance | 10-12 ohms | ~1.4 (good) | Maintain 1.4+ | 10.5-11.5 ohms |

**Data source:** Engineering specs + historical defect data + customer complaints

**Step 2: Baseline Process Capability (Weeks 1-4, for each product line)**

- Produce 30-50 sample units of each product under normal conditions
- Measure CTQ parameters (use calibrated gauges, SPC software)
- Calculate mean, standard deviation, Cpk
- **If Cpk <1.33:** Process not capable; root cause = operator training gap, tooling wear, material issue, design flaw. Identify + fix before production at scale.
- **If Cpk ≥1.33:** Process capable; establish control limits on SPC chart

**Step 3: Operator Training (Month 2-3)**

*Training curriculum for production operators:*
1. **Why SPC matters:** Defects cost money (rework, customer returns); catching early saves time + cost
2. **How to measure:** Use provided gauges (calipers, pressure meter, etc.); measurement technique standardized; practice 5 times until repeatable
3. **How to plot on SPC chart:** Manual chart (paper) or digital (tablet app); plot data point; check if within control limits
4. **When to stop the line:**
   - If point falls outside ±3σ control limit (red zone): **STOP immediately; call supervisor**
   - If 2 consecutive points in ±2σ zone (yellow zone): **PAUSE; discuss with quality tech**
   - If 6 consecutive points trending upward/downward: **Potential drift; investigate**
5. **Root cause conversation:**
   - Operator + Quality Tech + Supervisor discuss: "What changed? Tooling? Material? Procedure? Operator fatigue?"
   - Adjust (tool reset, material lot swap, operator break, procedure clarification)
   - Resume production; SPC chart reset
6. **Certification:** Operator sign-off on training; competency check (observe 5 measurement cycles)

**Step 4: Pilot Implementation (Months 4-8)**

- Select 2-3 highest-volume product lines
- Implement SPC on 1-2 CTQ parameters per product
- Operators measure every 10th unit; plot on chart; pause if out-of-control
- Quality Tech available on-site (30 hours/week) to support troubleshooting
- **Target:** Achieve Cpk ≥1.33 on all CTQ parameters; reduce defects by 40-50%
- **If successful:** Roll out to all product lines (Months 9-12)

**Step 5: Scale to All Product Lines (Months 13-24)**

- Phased rollout (1-2 new product lines per month)
- Hire 2 additional Quality Technicians (SPC specialists) to support operators
- Automate data collection (SPC software integrates with WMS; no manual charting)
- Monthly Cpk review with Production + Quality leadership

**Tools & Software Needed:**
- **SPC charting software:** JMP, Minitab, or open-source alternative (Graphpad Prism) = $500-2,000/license
- **Measurement equipment:** Calibrated digital calipers (±0.01mm), pressure meters, electrical testers = $3,000-5,000 per line
- **Operator training materials:** Posters, job aids, online video = $2,000-3,000 (one-time)
- **Quality Tech time:** 2 FTE @ $60K loaded = $120K/year (includes training, troubleshooting, data analysis)

**Budget:** ~$200K Year 1 (training + software + measurement equipment + tech hiring); $120K/year ongoing

---

#### 2.1.3 Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Review Process

**Problem:** Many defects originate in design (tolerances too tight, assembly ambiguous, materials not validated). Quality gate can't prevent design flaws.

**Solution:** Implement DFM checklist before design sign-off; catch issues early.

**DFM Review Checklist (to be completed for every new product or significant redesign):**

| Category | Review Questions | Owner | Gate Pass Criteria |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tolerance & Fit** | Are tolerances achievable with available equipment? Is Cpk ≥1.33 possible? Have we tested proto with worst-case tolerances? | Design Eng + Process Eng | All tolerances shown with Cpk basis; Design Eng confident in process capability (documented) |
| **Assembly** | Can assembly be done in <X seconds per unit (vs. current standard)? Are there ambiguous steps? Can assembly be done by average operator? | Design Eng + Production | Assembly procedure written; 3-person pilot assembly completed; time <target; no re-do required |
| **Material Sourcing** | Are materials available from qualified suppliers with <8 week lead time? Are there single-source risks? | Procurement + Design | Dual source identified for each critical material; supplier quality history reviewed (defect rate <1%, on-time delivery >98%) |
| **Test & Certification** | Does design allow for required testing (pressure, electrical, environmental)? Can test be done without disassembly? | Quality + Design | Test procedure drafted; proto tested; all parameters measureable; certification path clear |
| **Cost & Sustainability** | Does design optimize for cost? Are there scrap-prone features? | Operations + Design | BOM cost reviewed; scrap rate estimated <2% of material cost; labor cost estimate within ±10% of similar products |

**Governance:** DFM gate = design can't move to production until checklist complete + sign-off from Design + Production + Quality.

**Timeline:** Add 1-2 weeks to design cycle (before tooling ordered); saves 3-5 weeks in rework later.

---

### 2.2 SUPPLIER SYNCHRONIZATION: MOVE FROM REACTIVE TO PROACTIVE PROCUREMENT

#### 2.2.1 Rolling Demand Planning & Supplier Collaboration

**Current State (Reactive):**
```
Customer Order (Week 0) → PO issued to suppliers (Week 0) → Supplier lead time 8-10 weeks → Component arrives (Week 8-10) → Assembly starts → Production queue (total 14 weeks)
```

**Proposed State (Proactive):**
```
Demand Forecast (12-week rolling, updated monthly) → Supplier confirms line items (8 weeks out) → Supplier commits to ship date + safety stock buffer → Assembly starts by Week 6-7 → Production queue reduces (total 9-10 weeks)
```

---

#### 2.2.2 Implementation: Demand Forecasting & Supplier Tiering

**Step 1: Sales Forecasting Process (Months 1-2)**

*Current state:* Sales order-by-order; no advance planning shared with Operations/Procurement.

*New process:*
- **Sales forecast (12-week rolling window):** Sales manager + Account executives prepare monthly forecast of expected orders (by product, quantity, likely month)
  - Forecast accuracy target: ±20% for Months 1-4, ±30% for Months 5-8 (typical for industrial equipment)
  - Confidence level captured: "High confidence" (firm quote) vs. "Medium" (proposal stage) vs. "Low" (exploratory)
- **Operations translates forecast into component demand:** For each SKU in forecast, calculate BOM components required
  - Example: If forecasting 50 units of Product A in May, Operations calculates: Motors needed: 50 units, Control boards needed: 100 units (redundancy), etc.
- **Procurement uses forecast to drive supplier conversations (8 weeks ahead of expected delivery)**

**Step 2: Supplier Tiering & Segmentation (Month 1)**

Classify suppliers by criticality + lead time:

| Supplier Tier | Characteristics | Lead Time | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Critical Long-Lead (Tier 1)** | Single or few sources; 8-12 week lead times; high cost; limited supplier capacity; examples: specialty motors, control boards, castings | 8-10 weeks | Implement formal demand planning; quarterly business reviews; capacity allocation agreement; safety stock program |
| **Standard Lead (Tier 2)** | Multiple sources; 4-6 week lead times; moderate cost; available supply | 4-6 weeks | Monthly forecasting; PO confirmation 6 weeks out; standard terms |
| **Short Lead (Tier 3)** | Multiple local suppliers; 1-2 week lead times;
